definition: To formally give up a position of power, or to fail to carry out a duty you are responsible for.
example: In the fairy tale, the weary king decides to abdicate so that his daughter can rule.
nuance: Unlike resign, abdicate suggests giving up something you were expected to keep, such as a throne or a duty, and it often carries blame.
prompt: A team captain is deciding whether to keep leading during a losing season.
options: Rather than abdicate her role, the captain scheduled extra practices for the team.
Eager to take charge, the captain stepped forward to abdicate command of the whole team.
The captain plans to abdicate for a longer season when she meets with league officials.
On every corner kick, the captain will abdicate the ball to the fastest striker.
reasons: She keeps her leadership role and acts on it instead of walking away from it.
Taking charge is the reverse of giving up a position of authority.
Arguing in favor of something is advocating, a different word; abdicating means surrendering a role.
Passing a ball is a physical act, not giving up a post or a responsibility.

practice.prompt: The treasurer of a chess club stops checking the club's accounts for a whole year.
options: By ignoring the accounts, the treasurer seemed to abdicate a basic duty of the job.
The treasurer will abdicate the club's savings by spending them on fancy new boards.
To abdicate his duties, the treasurer reviewed every receipt twice each month.
At the meeting, the treasurer moved to abdicate the old dues rule and declare it void.
reasons: Neglecting the main task of an office is a clear case of walking away from a responsibility.
Wasting money is squandering it; the word refers to giving up a duty or position, not spending.
Checking receipts carefully means doing the job, the opposite of abandoning it.
Canceling a rule is abrogating, a look-alike word; the treasurer is not giving up any role.
